title: Straight answers
points: $933k — The schools need $932,664 more next year than the town can give them. That is the whole problem, in one number. | 2.68% — The things schools buy get 5.18% more expensive each year. State law lets the town collect about 2.5% more each year. Nobody overspent — the two numbers are simply different. | $573k — That difference opens a brand new hole every year, of roughly $572,745 to $788,595, whether or not you closed the last one. | 1 yr — So no single cut fixes this. point_1: $933k — The schools need $932,664 more next year than the town can give them. That is the whole problem, in one number.
point_2: 2.68% — The things schools buy get 5.18% more expensive each year. State law lets the town collect about 2.5% more each year. Nobody overspent — the two numbers are simply different.
point_3: $573k — That difference opens a brand new hole every year, of roughly $572,745 to $788,595, whether or not you closed the last one.
point_4: 1 yr — So no single cut fixes this. Every answer in the table below — sports, fees, administrators, pay, insurance — buys one year at most, and then the question comes back larger.

title: The budget gap
points: Cutting every extra still funded — $376,207 — covers 40% of next year’s gap, once. | ~90% — Contracts, insurance and law set about 90% of the budget; after the extras, only classroom positions are big enough to cut. | 2.25 pts — The published cost increase is 3.98%; the one that comes back every year is 6.23%.
point_1: Cutting every extra still funded — $376,207 — covers 40% of next year’s gap, once.
point_2: ~90% — Contracts, insurance and law set about 90% of the budget; after the extras, only classroom positions are big enough to cut.
point_3: 2.25 pts — The published cost increase is 3.98%; the one that comes back every year is 6.23%.
